speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, I beg to move, "That the total sum to be allocated for Head M of the Estimates be reduced by $100".

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This paper provides a useful forward view on the likely fiscal trends in the next decade, as we debate Budget 2023 and our longer-term positioning in the new era.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We know that these spending, once introduced, can only grow bigger and are unlikely to be reversed.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Cutting costs to balance a Budget is increasingly not a possible option.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: We need to expand and diversify our revenue sources, and hence, growing our economy and growing our reserves for the annuities to help fund the Budget is an imperative.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While we cannot cut costs to greatness, we should do our level best to ensure public funds are well spent, spend effectively and are achieving the desired outcomes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Given this backdrop, I would like to hear from the Minister, how MOF intends to maintain fiscal sustainability, even as our spending needs continue grow?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In the Budget Statement debate, I expressed concerns about cost pressures faced by businesses and the need to step-up the overall productivity.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Many companies transact and do businesses with the Government and the way the Government agencies conduct its operations, and the processes involved, can have a significant impact on cost to the businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: While we must be digitally inclusive when dealing with individuals; especially the seniors, we can aim for greater digital pervasiveness when doing businesses with the enterprises.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: There must be continued obsession to improve processes and users' experience; whether through greater digital adoptions or process streamlining.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: In this regard, I would like to ask if MOF has any plans to make doing businesses with Government even more seamless, less time consuming and lower the costs?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government is a major buyer of goods and services, and many SMEs and start-ups have innovative solutions and product offerings that can be of value to the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, I would like to also ask, how can MOF and the public agencies better support and facilitate the growth of SMEs when they participate in Government procurements?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: This is a laudable effort and a major undertaking for the Government.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Can I ask the Ministry: how is MOF supporting the whole-of-Government in this effort?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government and MOF can also play a significant role helping businesses build green capabilities and capture growth opportunities, given the buying power of the public sector.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So, can I seek an update from Minister in this area?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: The Government can be a catalyst to spur more innovative social solutions and contribute to a stronger social compact.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: So may I ask the Minister: how is MOF is supporting the development of the social sector?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: And finally, in this Committee of Supply (COS), can I also seek an update on the various policy measures in place, to encourage philanthropy and volunteerism?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Bukit Panjang)
text: Earlier in the debate, Assoc Prof Jamus Lim commented that the fiscal stance for Budget 2023 is a contractionary one.

speaker: Mr Chairman
text: Mr Leong Mun Wai, you can take your two cuts together please.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, I have questions for the Minister of Finance.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Contingencies Fund was created for urgent and unforeseen expenditure.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Three, are there financial projections available, to determine the amount or transfer to the endowment and trust funds, and is the actual spending from the funds included in the Budget, in the year when the spending was made or is it off-balance sheet of the Budget?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Fifth, based on what is given in the Budget, can the Minister confirm, what are the total financial assets as of 31 March 2022 and what is the net investment return (NIR) estimated for fiscal year 2023?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Mr Chairman, the People's Action Party (PAP) Government and some of its MPs like to invoke the claim of raiding of the reserves to attack alternative policy ideas and proposals put up by the Opposition.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In order to have a more productive debate in this House, it will be helpful to have an understanding of what constitutes "raiding of reserves".

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And secondly, the purpose of the expenditure, any proposal that passes these two criteria, where the amount involved is small relative to the reserves, or even the NIR, and serves an important purpose, should not be accused of raiding the reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During the debate, I explained that the Affordable Homes Scheme will only defer the accumulation of reserves, because the deferred land cost will be collected when the flat is sold in the future.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And even if, the whole deferred land cost of about $3 billion per year is not collectable, it is only 6.4% of NIR and 12.8% of NIRC.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We do not even need to use our reserves, so we have passed criteria one comfortably.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For criteria two, the money is to be spent on an important and noble purpose, which is to make the Housing and Development Board (HDB) flat affordable and accessible for every Singaporean, of each generation.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It will allow Singaporeans to retire comfortably, without having to sell his flat or downgrade.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The financial security accorded is expected to unleash the innovative and entrepreneurial spirit in Singaporeans, and you would be able to better compete with the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Hence, based on the two criteria above, the affordable home scheme is an example of an alternative policy that does not constitute a raiding of reserves according to my definition.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I hope to hear from the Minister what does she think.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In the future, from my point of view, if the Government makes such accusations again, I will call them baseless allegations.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, my cut today refers to my exchange with Minister Indranee Rajah during the debate on the Carbon Pricing (Amendment) Bill.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It would also seem that the Government can and does deem the President's approval to have been given or not given without necessarily referring the matter to the President.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: As I understand the statement, she did say that the President's approval or non-approval could be, to all practical intents and purposes, deemed to have been given by the Cabinet.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: The role of the President in this regard does not seem to serve any check or balance function.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: What function then does it serve?One asks oneself what possible purpose could be served by such a procedural requirement baked into the Constitution.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: I can see no benefit to the body politic.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Making it known that the President's approval is deemed by the Cabinet in certain domains as happened in November last year does not serve to enhance the prestige and standing of the Office of the President in the eyes of the public.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: In fact, to the contrary, this practice of "deemed approval" risks being seen by the public as involving the Office of President in a rubber-stamping or box-ticking exercise.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: It serves no constructive purpose and undermines the standing of the President.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: If there is no real reason for such provisions, will the Government do away with these provisions at some point in the future, given that there are no upsides but only downsides?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Aljunied)
text: Unless there are some upsides I cannot fathom right now and which the Government can explain.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat, you can take both your cuts together.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In refining our checks on public spending, we must be cautious not to add further unnecessary or disproportionate bureaucracy as this will erode whatever savings we achieve from public procurement.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, while I agree there is still room to invest in automated systems and training to eliminate human error, adding another one to two levels of approving authorities may be an inefficient and even ineffective solution.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Whether under Emergency Procurement or normal procurement procedures, how does Ministry of Finance (MOF) ensure that public spending is scrutinised adequately to enable cost savings and what efforts are being undertaken to ensure prudent spending at all levels across the Government?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How are larger projects, for example, like infrastructure spending being monitored?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mr Chairman, the public sector is a major buyer of goods and services.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Set up in June 2000, GeBIZ was ahead of its time and was followed by many other e-procurement systems in other countries aimed at enhancing transparent competition and lowering the barriers for small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to pitch for valuable Government contracts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How can GeBIZ be further augmented to help businesses save time and money in their transactions with Government agencies?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: For example, we can explore adding new features to integrate any industry briefings, tender briefings or site show-rounds with the relevant tender opportunities; and to engage with the procurement agency regarding any tender clarifications.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Besides ensuring that the public sector obtains the best value-for-money, public procurement can serve the role of supporting the growth of promising SMEs and startups who have innovative solutions.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In line with our strategy of supply diversification for resilience, can MOF’s "value-for-money" metric accommodate this aim?

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: And what else can MOF do to help support the growth of promising SMEs through Government procurement?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should look for ways to further grow SMEs to large local enterprises (LLEs) to increase their scale and per capita contribution to our economy.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Accordingly, I call upon MOF to facilitate more procurement opportunities for SMEs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What can MOF do to help support the growth of promising SMEs through Government procurements?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we further ensure that more such opportunities are made available for SMEs?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Currently, a gap exists in contract value threshold for a request for quotations and tender.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, can the Government review financial grading requirements for certain types of products and services to crowd source more innovative solutions?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Some of these solutions can be provided by startups who may not meet the required financial grading due to the stage of their companies' growth.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By doing so, the Government can tap on new innovations.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Tenders do take significant time and resources for SMEs and startups which translates to opportunity costs.

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In relation to the point on opportunity costs, can the Government streamline its processes to help businesses save time and money in their transactions with Government agencies?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Can these digital solutions and innovations in turn encourage more efficient ways of doing business between companies and their suppliers and customers?

speaker: Mr Edward Chia Bing Hui (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, increasing access to public sector contracts and reducing cost and time to transact with Government at the tender and operational stages can significantly help grow our SMEs and startups.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is a significant commitment and a non-trivial one to achieve, especially in the midst of an energy crisis.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many decarbonisation technologies are already ready today, but the speed of rollout depends on various other factors like infrastructure upgrades, business model and regulatory changes.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: While other decarbonisation technologies, especially in hard to abate sectors of the economy, are not yet available at scale today.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Until technologies like green hydrogen or CCUS become cost competitive versus carbon intensive alternatives, it will be difficult to mobilise the capital needed to scale and bring them down the cost curve over time.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Governments must play their part to incentivise the flow of investment into these climate solutions, and the transition to these solutions given their cost disadvantage.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: By giving incentives to reduce the “green premium”, and through innovative risk sharing and financing structures, including public-private partnerships, Government can be the catalyst for a faster transition.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The US Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) of August 2022 has been billed as the largest piece of federal legislation to address climate change.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In Singapore the Government has many fiscal and non-tax levers to drive the transition which it has used, such as carbon tax, and funding for research.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Given recent developments, can the Minister provide an update on how MOF is supporting the transition to net zero?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Chairman, we anticipate a tighter fiscal space in the coming years.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is scope for wealthy families, businesses and individuals to contribute meaningfully through philanthropy to our rising needs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Unlike a conventional system that relies heavily on taxation and redistribution, philanthropy offers the added benefit of strengthening our social compact.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The number of wealth owners and family offices in Singapore continues to grow at a healthy rate.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many of them have expressed interest to give back to society, both in Singapore and regionally.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As we encourage philanthropy to continue to grow, it is important to ask what types of philanthropy will have the greatest impact on Singapore.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Prof Rob Reich of Stanford University has argued that philanthropy has a special role in discovery and experimentation, serving as society’s "risk capital" to foster innovation in important areas that deemed to carry too much risk for Government or private sector appetites.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As such, philanthropy can be catalytic and complementary to public funding – it can identify and support high-impact opportunities that are in its early stage.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: When the solutions are proven, philanthropists can partner with the public sector to scale them up.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is also important to identify the most pressing areas of need where philanthropy can have the greatest impact.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Take climate change as an example – it is an existential imperative, and the negative effects of climate change will also exacerbate other areas of need, such as global health and pandemics, inequality and displacement of communities.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They can quickly deploy unrestricted funds in response to urgent problems such as natural disasters, back high-risk ventures, convene stakeholders and promote collaboration, develop and share research, and support large-scale implementation of climate solutions.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, I want to ask how can the Government foster support and public-private partnerships, both in Singapore and overseas, for such philanthropic causes, to address some of society’s most pressing challenges and issues?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In promoting philanthropy, we must also consider policies across the continuum of doing good, which is wide-ranging and can include venture philanthropy, concessionary capital and impact investing – a broad range continuum.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many wealth owners, especially those in the next generation, are looking towards these newer and more innovative approaches, sometimes referred to as “moon-shot” philanthropy.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: So, we must also recognise that beyond grant making, there are other ways to give back such as volunteerism and the contribution of skills and networks.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As the Government develops more initiatives and policies to promote philanthropy, how can it promote more diverse ways of doing good?

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Members for their questions and suggestions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa and Mr Saktiandi Supaat asked how the Government ensures fiscal sustainability and spend prudently within our means.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides the audits by the Auditor-General’s Office and our internal auditors, MOF conducts regular reviews of Ministries’ budgets to identify areas for improvement and ensures every Ministry uses its allocated resources efficiently and effectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Even as our expenditures grow further and exceed 20% of GDP by 2030, our Government expenditure as a percentage of GDP is significantly lower than most developed countries.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: At the same time, we are able to achieve positive economic and social outcomes for Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: One example is how we reduce the costs of major Government infrastructure projects by applying a stringent cost-effectiveness evaluation together with experts from the private sector and academia.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This $1 billion saved means we can put it to good use and meet our spending needs in other areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government also looks out for other forms of savings by integrating different projects to maximise the synergies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, the upcoming East Coast Integrated Depot, which incorporates three MRT depots and one bus depot, saved about 44 hectares of land.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is twice the land size of Changi Airport’s Terminal 4 or equivalent to approximately 60 football fields.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This approach also reduces the need for agencies to call separate tenders and quotations, saving at least 100,000 man-hours a year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government will continue to implement pro-business policies and measures and provide an environment that enables them to grow and succeed.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Besides supporting businesses through our economic agencies and via a comprehensive suite of grants and incentives for innovation, productivity improvements and skills-upgrading, there are two additional areas where MOF’s work benefit our companies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: First, by simplifying Government rules and processes, we enable businesses to save time and money when they transact with Government.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Second, by helping businesses build capabilities to enhance their competitiveness and access new opportunities, both locally and abroad.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We recently launched eGuarantee@Gov, a simple and secure digital process for businesses and individuals to provide a banker’s guarantee or insurance bond to Government agencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Businesses can apply for an eGuarantee from over 20 participating financial institutions online for direct submission to Government agencies within a day.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: With eGuarantee@Gov, there is no longer a need to visit a bank to purchase a physical copy of the guarantee or to pay for courier services to deliver it.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The new arrangement is quicker, better and cheaper.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We expect up to 4,000 eGuarantees to be lodged in 2023, resulting in overall savings for all stakeholders of about $500,000 per year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is also scope in the future for eGuarantees to extend to commercial transactions between businesses and their suppliers and customers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOF and the Ministry of Trade and Industry (MTI) will work with the financial institutions and trade association and chambers to encourage adoption of eGuarantees for such transactions.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Just as the use of PayNow for digital payments has allowed businesses and individuals to enjoy lower transaction costs and time savings compared to the traditional method of using cheques, the adoption of eGuarantees can bring about benefits compared to the current method of providing physical bank guarantees.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Next, MOF removed the requirement for businesses with annual turnover of less than $5 million to submit audited accounts when applying for Government Supplier Registration.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This benefits about 2,400 small and medium enterprises (SMEs) annually, with estimated cost savings of around $4.5 million per year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOF continually makes improvements to GeBIZ, the Government-wide procurement system.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For instance, about 3,000 businesses can benefit from the Supplier File Repository by the end of this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Businesses no longer need to submit the same financial statements and company profile when responding to different Government quotations and tenders.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will also consider the features that Mr Saktiandi mentioned for future improvements.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Such software provides many productivity benefits for businesses, as they can automatically generate and file their corporate income tax computations and returns.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This process takes only 15 minutes compared to the estimated eight hours required for manual preparation and submission.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Moving on to the next area of how MOF supports businesses to develop capabilities for growth.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We will continue to simplify our processes for suppliers, including SMEs, to participate in Government tenders while maintaining a level-playing field for all businesses and achieving value-for-money procurement outcomes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For procurement below $90,000, financial track record is not required.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, there is no requirement to provide security deposits.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Winning Government contracts gives SMEs the opportunity to build up their track records, develop capabilities and capacity to tap into new growth areas.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOF will work with representatives from Singapore Business Federation and the Association of Small and Medium Enterprises, as well as Government agencies on the design of Tender Lite.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We believe this approach of Government and industry working together as partners will bring about win-win outcomes and allow us to move faster and innovate new solutions more effectively.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: My colleagues and I are keen to continue the partnership with our industry partners beyond Tender Lite and extend the collaboration to other subsequent areas of work that will benefit our businesses.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Members such as Mr Derrick Goh have highlighted during the Budget debate that Government can help prepare SMEs for new requirements and opportunities in environmental sustainability.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The public sector is supporting our suppliers’ efforts to adopt greener practices which are increasingly in demand by other major buyers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Over the years, the Government has incorporated environmental sustainability requirements into our procurement such as requiring information and communication technology (ICT) equipment and air conditioners to meet energy efficiency standards.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government will further engage the industry stakeholders on the details of these measures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Another capability that is increasingly sought after is sustainability reporting.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Businesses that can provide good sustainability-related information can gain competitive advantage, expand into markets and potentially access cheaper funds through green financing.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: To drive sustainability reporting efforts for the industry, Accounting and Corporate Regulatory Authority (ACRA) and the Singapore Exchange Regulation established the Sustainability Reporting Advisory Committee in June 2022.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Committee will embark on its public consultations later this year.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Businesses also need to accelerate their pace of digitalisation, a point which Mr Liang made.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government will implement InvoiceNow as the default e-invoice submission channel for all Government vendors within the next few years.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Using InvoiceNow will help businesses improve efficiency and reduce cost, by eliminating the need for manual processing and it also reduces errors.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Businesses transacting on InvoiceNow can save $8 per invoice compared to the manual process.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: InvoiceNow also facilitates the direct transmission of invoices in a structured and standardised digital format that is accepted internationally across finance systems, and this helps businesses access overseas markets more easily.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Today, about 55,000 businesses have adopted InvoiceNow, supported by 200 service providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I encourage more businesses to come on board.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Philanthropy and volunteerism are key elements for building a strong social compact.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There is something intangible and different in how we build up the character of our society, when people go beyond what they are required to contribute under our fair and progressive tax and benefits system, where everyone contributes something and those who are better off contribute more.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Many Singaporeans and also foreigners and companies who are based here, have an interest in philanthropy and are keen to help others in society.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: We have been strengthening our ecosystem to encourage their contributions and participation to maximise the positive impact to our local communities.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: This is a good way to keep our society cohesive and strengthen our solidarity as one united people.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: Not only through taxation and redistribution which are done through policies and laws but also through philanthropy and volunteerism which come from willing hands and loving hearts.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: MOF provides funding support for many community and ground-up programmes which contribute to the development of the social sector.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: There are many existing efforts by agencies working with intermediaries like the Community Foundation of Singapore and ComChest, as well as beneficiaries to link up donors with suitable charitable causes.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: I have also met wonderful people such as those from Utama and Majurity Trust, who started initiatives to help raise donations from high net worth individuals and corporations to fund worthy social causes like caring for vulnerable seniors and providing opportunities for children from lower-income families.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government provides broad-based support in the form of 250% tax deductions for qualifying donations to Institutions of a Public Character (IPCs) and the Corporate Volunteer Scheme (CVS) supports volunteerism efforts by businesses in IPCs.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: The Government also provides matching grants to encourage charitable giving.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Finance (Mr Chee Hong Tat)
text: For example, we allocated a top-up of $100 million to the Tote Board’s Enhanced Fundraising Programme which in turn provides dollar-for-dollar matching on eligible donations received by charities.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Chairman, I will be responding to the cuts filed by Mr Leon Perera and Mr Leong Mun Wai.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Leon Perera asked about the processes for obtaining the President’s recommendation to move a Bill, or amendments to a Bill tabled in Parliament.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If the recommendation is provided, then it shows that the legislation or amendment has the Government's support.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is different from the other provisions of the Constitution where the President acts upon his or her discretion, for example, in relation to draws on past reserves or the appointment of certain key appointment holders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where the requirement in Article 59(2) is triggered and the Government does not support the Bill or amendment, there is no need to seek or to advise the President not to provide the recommendation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is sufficient to inform the House that the Bill or amendment does not have the President's recommendation in accordance with the Standing Orders.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Where the Government supports the Bill or the amendment, the Government will seek the recommendation of the President and formally advise the President to provide such recommendation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This requirement for Government support before financial legislation can be passed is a standard arrangement of many Commonwealth parliamentary democracies, although the mechanisms may vary.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In Singapore, it is done through the mechanism of the President's recommendation, as I have explained.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In New Zealand, where a Bill or amendment "would have more than a minor impact on the Government's fiscal aggregates if it became law", the government may issue a "Financial veto certificate" to state that it does not concur with the Bill or amendment, in which event, such Bill or amendment cannot be passed.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In Canada, this is done by requiring the royal recommendation, which may only be obtained by a Minister, to be conveyed to Parliament.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: While the mechanisms may vary from country to country, the principle underpinning them is the same.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That is to say, a Bill or an amendment with financial implications cannot be passed if the government of the day does not support it, in recognition of the principle that responsibility for financial matters lies with the Government.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: So, earlier, when Mr Leon Perera talked about "deeming", there is no "deeming" involved.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If the Government does not support the Bill or the amendment, the Government would not even need to put it to the President.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: But if the Government supports it, then the Government will put it to the President with the requisite advice and the recommendation would be signified in Parliament.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Hence, the Council of Presidential Advisers (CPA) is also not engaged because this is not a discretionary function of the President.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The President may consult the CPA for the discretionary functions.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This is provided for in Standing Order 67(1).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Members may recall that a few days ago, I introduced the Supply Bill.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: When I introduced the Supply Bill, I signified to the Chamber that I had the President's recommendation.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: In the case of a private Member's Bill, the Minister for Finance has to inform the Speaker whether the President's recommendation is required under Article 59(2).

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If no such recommendation has been obtained, the Speaker shall not allow the Motion for leave to introduce the Bill to be moved.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The same procedure applies to amendments proposed to Bills.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: One more thing I should add, which is that if a Member intends to propose a Bill or amendments to a Bill, which make provision directly or indirectly for the list of financial matters listed in Article 59(2), he or she should inform the Ministry or Minister with oversight of the matters in the Bill or amendment as soon as possible and ideally no later than the time of filing the relevant notices with Parliament so that the relevant assessments and steps can be taken.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If the Member is not sure whether the matters in the Bill or amendment are caught by the provisions of Article 59(2), then all the more so it would be advisable to inform the relevant Ministry or Minister early.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I move on to Mr Leong Mun Wai's cuts.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Mr Leong did not provide the indication of these beforehand.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Normally in the gist of the Budget cuts, Members are asked to provide the gist.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I also do send out a notice, generally, to ask people to provide the gist of their cuts because it will then enable us to respond in a more considered or fuller manner.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: With respect to the five questions which basically were given on the spot, I will give such replies as I can.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: If the Member has any other things, it will have to be taken up separately.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I think the first question was on the termination of the Sports Hub.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: I would say in response the reason for the termination of the Sports Hub was addressed in the Ministry of Culture, Community and Youth (MCCY)'s Ministerial Statement in  August 2022.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For his second question on the SPH Media Trust, that is from the Ministry of Communications and Information (MCI)'s annual budget from FY2022 to FY2026.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: However, no money has been disbursed as Minister Josephine Teo had said in Parliament.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For his third question, disbursement figures from the Government statutory funds are in the Government Financial Statements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The disbursement figures for the funds under the Statutory Boards are included in their financial statements.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: This was answered earlier this month by Senior Minister of State Chee in a response to a Parliamentary Question.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: For the fifth question, I think the answers there can be found in the Budget Book.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Then, with regard to his last point about what is the definition of "raiding the reserves", Mr Chairman, it is not a term of art.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: Essentially, we have a framework on how the reserves are to be used.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is a simple principle that we adhere to.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: It is not necessary for me to go into a definitional argument.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The reasons and the rationale of when you can have a draw on the reserves are clear.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: A pandemic would be a good reason – when you are facing potential catastrophe and you have to save the economy, you have to save people.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: That is something that is built into the current framework.

speaker: The Second Minister for Finance (Ms Indranee Rajah)
text: The reserves can only be used with the agreement of the President.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Chairman, I thank the Minister for the reply.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: One is that given the kind of payments like the Sports Hub and also SPH Media Trust, where is a big payment to a third party, what is the procedure whereby the Parliament can come in and have oversight over such expenditure?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Meaning, how far can the Government just approve the expenditure, just like that?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: For example, now, we have this SINGA Bill where infrastructural projects that are more than $4 billion require – when it goes through the SINGA Bill, then it comes to Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: But does it mean that if in the future, there is a project where we need to terminate the project and it is a $4 billion payout, the Government just makes the decision like that without Parliament scrutinising the numbers?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The second question is, to your best knowledge as the Second Minister for Finance, what is the percentage of the endowment funds that are being paid out every year – as a percentage of the outstanding assets that these endowment funds have at the moment?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: The third question, with regards to the raiding of reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: Your question basically means – does it mean that as long as the Government has a set of rules, we cannot debate against that set of rules?

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: In this case, it is a set of rules regarding reserves management and the recording of the reserves.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: You can always say that what you have proposed is not in line with our reserve management policies but we can still discuss about it.

speaker: Mr Leong Mun Wai
text: There is no need to say right from the beginning, that this is a raiding the reserves and it is not only one time, but many many times by many people and over the mass media and all that.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Could we keep it concise so that others can ask their clarifications?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Therefore, there are quite a large scope of things which is under the authority of the Government.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, the debate that we just had, for example, the Budget debate we call it the Budget debate but actually, people forget what it actually is.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is a Motion to ask this House to approve the Government's financial policy.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: I think that is available to the Member as well.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: So, we have a whole series of checks and balances.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You have got the Constitution, which sets the framework.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The fiscal policy or financial policy is subject to Parliamentary approval and subject to debate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is also subject to independent audits by the Auditor-General's Office (AGO).

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The Public Accounts Committee also examines the Government's accounts and the AGO's report and calls on the relevant agencies to explain particular issues or to take corrective actions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: For the second question on the extent of funds paid out every year, since that is a very specific question requiring certain data, perhaps the Member can file a question on that.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The third question was, I think the Member put it this way – he said does it mean that if the Government has a set of rules, we cannot debate it because he said we can always say it is not in line.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: He also said that there was no need to say that it is raiding one time but all the time.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The first one – does it mean that we have a set of rules?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Does it mean that you cannot debate the rules?

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: You can suggest that it should be changed.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But so long as the rules are in place and so long as what is proposed is not in conformance with those rules and is a draw on the reserves, then it means that it falls outside or breaches, if you like, or it is not in accordance with the rules.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And if you want to debate whether that should or should not be the rule, that is entirely up to that Member's prerogative.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But if what you happen to be proposing does not fall within the rules, then the Government is entitled to say that it would be a draw or, put it in a slightly easier to understand form, it will be a raid on the reserves.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And secondly, Mr Leong suggested that there is no need to say raiding the reserves, not one time but many, many times.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The answer is that, if your proposals do actually intend to draw down the reserves not one time but many, many times, then, inevitably, it will draw the reaction that you are raiding not one time but many, many times.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: I often hear this feedback from the businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: The pain point is always that the Government rules can be quite cumbersome and some are unnecessary and the procedures can be quite inefficient.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Liang for asking this very important question.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: The Government deals with quite a lot of businesses: in our capacity as regulator, when they are applying for licence, they need our permit to operate; or as a buyer, when we procure services and then they are our suppliers.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: In both instances, there is scope for us to continue to look for ways in which we can do better in our interactions with businesses especially smaller businesses, the SMEs, because they do not have a lot of resources.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, when we design our licensing framework, when we design our rules and procedures, we also want to make sure that they are able to comply with not too much difficulty.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And my colleagues from the other Government Ministries and agencies, have also been embarking on this initiative.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: When you remove some of these, then they do not have to apply, do not have to pay.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: This is something we want to keep doing and it has to be a partnership with our businesses and our trade associations, because the Government may not know fully where are all the pain points and where are all the areas for improvement.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But from the users' point of view, the businesses will know.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: That is why I mentioned in my speech earlier that I want to work closely with SBF and ASME, not just to improve on the tender processes by introducing Tender Lite, which is one of the ways to help businesses, but also on other pro-business initiatives.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: The hon Member Mr Liang had suggested earlier on and, if I heard correctly, that so long as we have a positive NIRC, then the Budget must necessarily be expansionary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And, if so, since the NIRC has been consistently positive, at least since 2008, would that mean that he believes that over the past decade and a half, that we have never run a contractionary fiscal stance?

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: And I am wondering if the Minister of Finance or anyone from the Finance Ministry is willing to corroborate this characterisation.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: If what the Member meant was, so long as the sum of the NIRC and revenue is less than expenditure, then it is expansionary.

speaker: Assoc Prof Jamus Jerome Lim (Sengkang)
text: But since the NIRC has, in fact, been positive, this would actually mean an even greater surplus over expenditure, which would mean an even more contractionary budget, contrary to an expansionary one.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: My point was that our expenditures are way higher than the taxes that we collected from the system.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: In that regard, it is expansionary because we are spending more than that we collect from the taxes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: And in reference to the clarification earlier that the Member said that every dollar in the tax that the Government collected is taking out from the system.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: But, here, in our case, our expenditures are way above the revenue that we collect from taxes.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I have two clarifications for Senior Minister of State Chee, not on philanthropy because the question roughly is answered, but two clarifications regarding a debate brought up here.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: First, Senior Minister of State spoke about Government's effort to support businesses, especially SMEs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: So, how we pay them is going to be important.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Is that achievable, that request from Nominated Member of Parliament Ms Janet Ang?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: The Senior Minister of State spoke about that just now.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: I want to ask what happens if some SMEs have not put in place the necessary infrastructure?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har
text: Does that mean they cannot participate in Government procurement?

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: And this is a standard that I would say, is comparable, if not, better than some of the other governments and even private sector companies.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But we will want to work towards, where possible, to shorten the payment period.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: Because, as the Member correctly pointed out, this will directly benefit our SMEs in terms of cashflow.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: I would want to caveat that a little bit by saying that it depends really on the nature of the contract.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: There are some that are more straightforward – the service has been provided, the product has been delivered, everything is okay, we can try and speed it up.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But there are some that may require more evaluation because it is not so straightforward, or if the amounts are much bigger and we need to be careful, with due diligence, in order to ensure value for money and prudent spending.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: But larger amounts, more complex contracts, we may need to give the agencies a bit more time so that they also can safeguard the interests of public funds.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: I just have one clarification, and I appreciate her laying out the process for seeking the President's recommendation on Bills, with fiscal implications as well as speaking about areas of exercisable discretion and so on.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: My clarification is just about why there is a need to have this rather curious and complicated procedure, where for these matters, something is referred to the President, but then, the Cabinet instructs the President to act in a very prescriptive way and President has to act that way and then the Bill can move forward in Parliament.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It does not seem to serve any constructive purpose, in terms of time and the administrative effort and efficiency.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And moreover, would the Minister give some thought to the consideration I raised?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: There is a potential disamenity in keeping such arrangements in place which is that of the President being seen to be a part of this sort of procedure which involves box-ticking or rubber stamping.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: It does not really help the standing of the Office of the President and just seems unnecessary.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: Will the Government consider reforming this aspect of the Constitution to sort of do away with that procedural step.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: And before I resume my seat, I just want to say that it should be clear that we have debated in this Chamber before on the Workers' Party's position on the Presidency —

speaker: The Chairman
text: If you could keep it short on this point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera
text: That it should revert to a ceremonial Presidency.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Mr Chairman, I thank Mr Perera for his clarification.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But actually, this procedure is a very long-standing procedure, not just ours, but it is a feature of the Westminster model and parliamentary democracies.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: In other words, these procedures, you may call it elaborate.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is a polite way of coming to Parliament to say that you need the Government's support.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Many of the things which have its roots in parliamentary procedure from the Westminster model come from these – you could say, these courtesies of the past.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: The New Zealanders, as I described, are a little bit more direct about it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is just a government "veto certificate". "Nope" and that is it.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: But we are doing it in a polite way.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: We signify whether the President has given her recommendation.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: Whether or not the President gives her recommendation, would depend on whether or not the Government gives its support.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It does not in any way affect the standing of the President.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It was a very early feature of our Constitution.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And you will find it, if you check, you will find it in many different ways, shapes or forms in other Commonwealth jurisdictions.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: And so, it is not so much a question of box-ticking, certainly not the case.

speaker: Ms Indranee Rajah
text: It is very much a case of observing certain proprieties which are laid out and, in a way, that has a long-standing tradition.

speaker: The Chairman
text: We have to end it by 7.15 pm.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: I am just glad that we are discussing today about cost savings when our neighbour just released their budget and they are talking about cutting their deficits and reducing the government debt.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: My question is to Senior Minister of State Chee, in response to his answer to my cards.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: In regard to the scrutiny of infrastructure spending, he answered that question in terms of public accounts.

speaker: Mr Saktiandi Supaat
text: But, maybe, if Senior of Minister of State can share a bit more about our cost savings and our efforts from smaller projects, smaller to medium-term projects, and what additional sort of scrutiny and efforts to review those and how we can enhance on that front as well.

speaker: Mr Chee Hong Tat
text: So, we have been encouraging the Ministries and —

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Liang Eng Hwa, would you like to withdraw your amendment?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa
text: Allow me to thank Deputy Prime Minister Wong and our best-in-class MOF team for the reassuring as well as forward-looking Budget; and also thank you to Minister Indranee and Senior Minister Chee Hong Tat for responding to our cuts.
